newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Exports boost S.African non-farm economy.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Exports boost S.African non-farm economy.

text.p: Economists have upgraded forecasts for South African growth in 1997, thanks to an export-led recovery in manufacturing which will cut the current account gap, according to a Reuters survey released on Thursday.
But over the next three years the government is still expected to fall short of growth targets set out in last year's five-year macroeconomic strategy.

The quarterly survey of 23 local and international analysts, the first since the 1997/98 budget was unveiled on March 12, showed a consensus for real GDP growth of 2.4 percent this year, up from 2.2 percent forecast in late November.

That is broadly in line with the prediction of 2.5 percent made by Finance Minister Trevor Manuel in his budget but considerably less bullish than Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals' view of around 3.0 percent.
In 1998 and 1999 the economic upturn should gain momentum with GDP increasing 3.4 percent and 3.7 respectively, the survey showed.

Analysts said the economic fundamentals were now in place for solid growth after a brief downturn in the non-farm economy in 1996. But official goals of 2.9 percent growth in 1997, 3.8 percent in 1998 and 4.9 percent look over-optimistic.
"On the non-agriculture side 1997 will definitely be a much better year than last year," said Herman van Papendorp.
"Domestic demand is not very strong, so the focus will be on exports. We are entering an export-led growth phase."

Other analysts said the mediocre overall growth figure for 1997 disguised a strong recovery in the non-farm sector. Last year's growth was mainly due to exceptional rains and bumper harvests of crops, which distorted the underlying picture.
GDP growth in 1996 was 3.1 percent, only slightly less than the 3.4 percent increase in 1995, but output in the non-farm sector expanded a meagre 1.9 percent against 3.9 in 1995.

This year the tables will be turned with agriculture unable to match last year's performance leaving manufacturing and services as the main drivers, said Ben van Rensburg, economic policy director at the South African Chamber of Business.
"In order to achieve the 2.5 percent growth level we are predicting in 1997, the non-farm economy will have to grow at more than three percent," he said.

Johan Els of life assurance giant Old Mutual said the depreciation of the rand by 22 percent against a basket of currencies in 1996 would give a substantial boost to export-oriented manufacturing industries.
That, in turn, would cut the current account deficit on the balance of payments sharply, paving the way for a steadier currency in 1997 and 1998.
The consensus forecast for the current account gap in 1997 was 3.65 billion rand, down from 8.5 billion rand in 1996. In 1998 it was seen at 3.72 billion.
